description: How wind and solar exploded while coal crashed — U.S. installed power capacity, 2004–2024
youtube_description:
The Renewable Rush — U.S. power capacity race (2004–2024)

Chapters:
0:00 Intro — The moment the grid changed
0:24 2004 baseline: Coal still dominant (315 GW)
0:55 The early growth: Wind climbs from 6 GW to 60 GW by 2012
1:35 Solar infancy to boom: 0.3 GW (2004) → 170 GW (2024)
2:10 Coal decline: 315 GW (2004) → 200 GW (2024)
2:45 Natural gas surge: 380 GW (2004) → 580 GW (2024)
3:15 Nuclear steady, the slow churn (≈100 GW)
3:45 The tipping point: 2015–2024 — renewables accelerate
4:20 Visual summary & call to action
4:40 Sources & how we built these numbers

Story summary:
This chart race visualizes 21 years of U.S. installed electric capacity by fuel (2004–2024). Coal drops from 315 GW in 2004 to ~200 GW in 2024. Natural gas rises from ~380 GW to ~580 GW. Wind explodes from 6 GW to 150 GW; solar from 0.3 GW to 170 GW. Nuclear stays roughly flat near 98–101 GW. The result: renewable capacity goes from a rounding error in 2004 to a top contender in 2024.

Why this matters:
- Rapid cost declines in wind and solar, state-level mandates, and tax incentives drove deployment.
- Market forces and retirements pushed coal down; natural gas filled the flexibility gap.
- The grid mix shift impacts emissions, reliability planning, storage needs and policy.

Sources used (selected):
- U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) — Electric Power Annual & Capacity files
- American Wind Energy Association (AWEA) / American Clean Power
- Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) — U.S. Solar Market Insight
- Company & utility capacity filings and public reports

instagram_caption:
🚀 The renewable boom that broke the old grid — 2004 vs 2024 in one race. 

In 2004 coal sat at about 315 GW of U.S. installed capacity. By 2024 that number had fallen to ~200 GW — a roughly 36% drop. Natural gas went the other way: ~380 GW in 2004 to ~580 GW in 2024, a surge of 200 GW that kept lights on while the grid changed.

But the real story is wind and solar. Wind capacity went from a tiny 6 GW in 2004 to about 150 GW in 2024 — a 25x increase. Solar’s climb is even more dramatic on percentage terms: 0.3 GW in 2004 to roughly 170 GW in 2024. That’s not an incremental change — that’s a market remake. In two decades rooftop arrays, utility solar farms, and huge wind projects turned renewables from a curiosity into a central pillar of U.S. capacity.

Nuclear hardly moved — roughly 98–101 GW across the whole period — it stayed important but didn’t join the growth party. Meanwhile, coal retirements and lower utilization pushed its footprint down fast. By the late 2010s and into the 2020s, the combined rise of wind and solar began to visibly reshape the dispatch stack and policy debates around storage, transmission, and reliability.

This timeline is a showdown: one set of technologies (wind + solar) skyrockets, coal gets crushed, and gas fills the flexibility gap. Numbers to remember: Coal 315 → 200 GW, Gas 380 → 580 GW, Wind 6 → 150 GW, Solar 0.3 → 170 GW (2004 → 2024). What surprised you most — the speed of solar’s rise or the depth of coal’s fall? Tell me which year you think was the turning point and why.
